summary: 1934 40-foot L-4 tower near Stampede Pass; Aircraft Warning Service site 1942-43; airlifted to Camp Waskowitz in 1974, where it is used for school outdoor education.

access.note: Camp Waskowitz is operated by Highline Public Schools for an environmental learning program. Plan any visit through the school program.

events.note: 40-foot timber tower with an L-4 cab on a small peak near Stampede Pass
Activated for the Aircraft Warning Service on August 14, 1942; ground cabin built; deactivated September 15, 1943
Airlifted by helicopter to Camp Waskowitz as a permanent exhibit; sources differ on whether the whole tower or only the cab flew
Visitor noticed at least two concrete footings still on the original knoll

evidence.supports: built 1934 as a 40-foot timber L-4 tower on a small peak southeast of the pass; airlifted to Camp Waskowitz in 1974 as a permanent exhibit
evidence.quote: Built in 1934, this 40' treated timber L-4 tower, on a small peak 3/4 mile southeast of the pass, was airlifted by helicopter to Camp Waskowitz conservation camp near North Bend as a permanent exhibit in 1974.

evidence.supports: a smaller 20-foot L-4 tower stood about a mile north for a time
evidence.quote: There was also a 20' L-4 tower one mile to the north of the main lookout for a time.

evidence.supports: administered by the U.S. Forest Service
built in 1934 as a 40 foot wood tower with L-4 cab
evidence.quote: In 1934, the Stampede Lookout was built, a 40 foot wood tower with L-4 cab.

evidence.supports: views of the Green River valley to the west and the Keechelus valley to the east
evidence.quote: It had views of the Green River Valley to the west and the Keechelus Valley to the east.

evidence.supports: the site was used by the Aircraft Warning Service in 1942
evidence.quote: In 1942, the site was used by the Aircraft Warning Service.
It was activated on August 14 1942 and deactivated on September 15, 1943.

evidence.supports: activation and deactivation dates on the Forest Lookouts Washington page
ground cabin built because the tall tower was too cold and loud in the wind
evidence.quote: A ground cabin was built because the tall tower was too cold and loud in the wind.

evidence.supports: plans to destroy the tower; North Bend ranger Ken White arranged the airlift to Camp Waskowitz as an exhibit
evidence.quote: When plans came to destroy the forty foot timber L-4 tower, North Bend ranger Ken White got it airlifted by helicopter to Camp Waskowitz conservation camp as an exhibit

evidence.supports: the cab alone was airlifted and mounted on a new tower (conflicting account)
evidence.quote: 1974: The cab was airlifted by helicopter to Camp Waskowitz, where it was mounted on a new tower.

evidence.supports: at least two concrete footings still on the original site in 2014
evidence.quote: In 2014, I noticed at least 2 of the concrete footings still remain on site.

evidence.supports: Camp North Bend, also called Camp Waskowitz, was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1935
evidence.quote: Constructed by and for the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) in 1935

evidence.supports: Camp Waskowitz is operated by Highline Public Schools for an environmental learning program
evidence.quote: Camp Waskowitz is currently operated by Highline Public Schools for their Environmental Learning Program.

evidence.supports: the tower at Camp Waskowitz is used for educational purposes
evidence.quote: This tower is used for educational purposes.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Former Fire Lookout Sites page and WillhiteWeb say the whole 40-foot tower was airlifted. The Forest Lookouts Washington page says only the cab was flown and mounted on a new tower. The story reports both accounts and does not pick one.

notes_for_editor: The tower's current condition at Camp Waskowitz rests on an undated Forest Lookouts line that it is used for educational purposes; no recent visit or photo was found. Highline's own pages were not fetched. The access level 'restricted' is inferred from the school-program operation, not from a stated visitor policy. The 1942 entry is recorded as Aircraft Warning Service activation; the sources do not say how many people staffed the site. Wikipedia is used as a lead for the camp; its statements were not checked against the sources it cites.
